results.name: n1_set_mean_variance
results.description: Variance across one-example sets of each set's mean yes rate; observed > null means people's breadth of generalization still differs more between lone examples than the richness-gated doubt allows (observed < null: model over-differentiates lone examples).
results.code:
# name: n1_set_mean_variance
# description: Variance across one-example sets of each set's mean yes rate; observed > null means people's breadth of generalization still differs more between lone examples than the richness-gated doubt allows (observed < null: model over-differentiates lone examples).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values[one]
    u, inv = np.unique(s.values[one], return_inverse=True)
    m = np.bincount(inv, weights=r) / np.bincount(inv)
    return float(np.var(m))

results.name: n1_distance_gradient
results.description: For one-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example minus targets more than 30 away; observed > null means people's magnitude generalization from a lone example is steeper than the model's, observed < null shallower (model over-produces nearness).
results.code:
# name: n1_distance_gradient
# description: For one-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example minus targets more than 30 away; observed > null means people's magnitude generalization from a lone example is steeper than the model's, observed < null shallower (model over-produces nearness).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    e = pd.to_numeric(s.where(one, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    d = np.abs(t - e)
    near = one & (d <= 10) & (d > 0)
    far = one & (d > 30)
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: n1_round_example_gap
results.description: For one-example sets, overall yes rate when the lone example is a multiple of 5 minus when it is not; observed < null means people generalize less broadly from a round lone example than the model predicts (round examples read as a narrow multiples-of-5/10 rule), observed > null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: n1_round_example_gap
# description: For one-example sets, overall yes rate when the lone example is a multiple of 5 minus when it is not; observed < null means people generalize less broadly from a round lone example than the model predicts (round examples read as a narrow multiples-of-5/10 rule), observed > null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    e = pd.to_numeric(s.where(one, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    rnd = one & (e % 5 == 0)
    non = one & (e % 5 != 0)
    if rnd.sum() == 0 or non.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[rnd].mean() - r[non].mean())

results.name: n1_round_target_gap
results.description: For one-example sets, yes rate on targets that are multiples of 10 minus other targets; observed < null means people reject round targets from a lone example more than the model predicts (observed > null: model under-produces a round-target bonus).
results.code:

def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = one & (t % 10 == 0)
    b = one & (t % 10 != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:

results.name: n1_parity_match_gap
results.description: For one-example sets, yes rate on same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null means the model's flat-rate doubt still dilutes parity generalization from a lone example (observed < null: model over-weights parity).
results.code:
# name: n1_parity_match_gap
# description: For one-example sets, yes rate on same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null means the model's flat-rate doubt still dilutes parity generalization from a lone example (observed < null: model over-weights parity).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    e = pd.to_numeric(s.where(one, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    same = one & (t % 2 == e % 2)
    diff = one & (t % 2 != e % 2)
    if same.sum() == 0 or diff.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[diff].mean())

results.name: multi_above_below_asymmetry
results.description: On 2-4-example sets, yes rate on targets above the largest example minus yes rate on targets below the smallest; observed > null means people extend upward more readily than downward, an asymmetry the model's equal-width band under-produces (observed < null: model over-produces it).
results.code:
# name: multi_above_below_asymmetry
# description: On 2-4-example sets, yes rate on targets above the largest example minus yes rate on targets below the smallest; observed > null means people extend upward more readily than downward, an asymmetry the model's equal-width band under-produces (observed < null: model over-produces it).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    lo = ex.min(axis=1).values
    hi = ex.max(axis=1).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    above = (n >= 2) & (t > hi)
    below = (n >= 2) & (t < lo)
    if above.sum() == 0 or below.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[above].mean() - r[below].mean())

results.name: n1_small_target_gap
results.description: For one-example sets, yes rate on targets 1-10 minus targets 11-100; observed < null means people endorse very small targets from a lone example less than the model predicts (a magnitude/plausibility prior the model lacks), observed > null the reverse.
results.code:

# description: For one-example sets, yes rate on targets 1-10 minus targets 11-100; observed < null means people endorse very small targets from a lone example less than the model predicts (a magnitude/plausibility prior the model lacks), observed > null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = one & (t <= 10)
    b = one & (t > 10)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: multi_parity_violation_yes
results.description: On 2-4-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate on targets of the opposite parity; observed > null means people accept parity-violating targets more than the model (its shared-profile share is too strict), observed < null the model is too lenient.
results.code:
# name: multi_parity_violation_yes
# description: On 2-4-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate on targets of the opposite parity; observed > null means people accept parity-violating targets more than the model (its shared-profile share is too strict), observed < null the model is too lenient.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    par = ex % 2
    mx = par.max(axis=1).values
    mn = par.min(axis=1).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    sel = (n >= 2) & (mx == mn) & ((t % 2) != mn)
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[sel].mean())
